taxodist is an open-source project for retrieving ordered taxonomic lineages and measuring separation between nodes in a classification hierarchy. It is available as coordinated R, Python, and Julia packages and through an interactive web application.
The project addresses a practical need: a reproducible way to resolve taxon names, inspect their lineages, identify their most recent common ancestor, and construct labeled distance objects for downstream analysis.
By default, lineages come from The Taxonomicon, based on Systema Naturae 2000. Since version 1.1.0, they can also be retrieved from the Open Tree of Life reference taxonomy and the NCBI Taxonomy (see Taxonomic sources). The external sources remain responsible for the underlying classifications; taxodist retrieves, cleans, organizes, and compares those records.

title: About taxodist
text:
Methodological position
By default, the distance between distinct hierarchy nodes is the reciprocal of MRCA depth. Identical complete lineages receive distance zero. Within a connected hierarchy, this produces an ultrametric. Path-length, Wu–Palmer, and rank-based distances are available as explicit alternatives.
These values measure classification depth. They do not estimate evolutionary time, genetic or morphological divergence, phylogenetic branch length, or statistical support for ancestry. The interpretation of every analysis is conditional on the source classification and the intermediate nodes it records.
Version 0.6.0 formalized this distinction across the R package, Python package, application, reference data, and documentation. Version 0.7.0 optimized cached matrix construction. Version 0.8.0 added auditable resolution records, offline user-supplied classifications, and portable analysis bundles shared by all three implementations. Version 0.9.0 corrected retrieval and caching errors and added classification trees, distances between two sets of taxa, and the comparison of repeated analyses. Version 1.0.0, the first stable release, replaced the text-based lineage parser with one that reads the structure of each Taxonomicon page, retained the rank of every node, added alternative distance metrics and the taxonomic distinctness indices of Clarke and Warwick, and froze the metric definitions and the bundle format for the 1.x series. Version 1.1.0 added the Open Tree and NCBI taxonomies as alternative lineage sources, the comparison of analyses across sources, and community analyses: the taxonomic dissimilarities of Clarke, Somerfield and Chapman between samples and the NRI and NTI effect sizes of Webb et al.

title: About taxodist
text:
Project history
The project began with a general question: how can the shared hierarchical position of any two named organisms be retrieved and compared programmatically?
Early development focused on resolving names and parsing the deeply nested classification exposed by The Taxonomicon. Subsequent releases added matrix operations, lineage comparison, cache persistence, visualization, multivariate helpers, offline reference data, Python and Julia implementations with matching distance semantics, and diversity indices.
The project remains deliberately focused on classification-based analysis. It does not attempt to replace curated phylogenies, sequence-based inference, divergence-time estimation, or specialized taxonomic name services.

title: Bundle format
text: A taxodist bundle is a single JSON file that stores a complete analysis: how every input name was resolved, the lineages (and their ranks) that were used, the distance matrix, the metric definition, and where the data came from. Bundles are written by write_taxodist_bundle(), read by read_taxodist_bundle(), and compared with compare_bundles() in all three languages. A bundle written in one language is read by the other two without differences.

title: Bundle format
text:
Versioning policy








Schema
Written by
Notes




1.0
taxodist 0.8.0 and 0.9.0
Reciprocal metric only; no ranks


1.1
taxodist 1.0.0 and 1.1.0
Adds the metric choice (and, for "ranked", its rank levels) and lineage_ranks




Versions 1.0.0 and 1.1.0 write schema 1.1; version 1.1.0 did not change the format.
Every 1.x release reads schema 1.0 and 1.1. A schema 1.0 bundle must use the reciprocal metric (inverse_mrca_depth).
The bundle format and the metric definitions are stable for the 1.x series: later 1.x releases continue to read bundles written by 1.0.0. A file whose schema_version is not 1.0 or 1.1 is rejected.

title: Bundle format
text:
Validation
Beyond the JSON Schema, readers and writers check that candidate counts match the candidates, that lineage_depth matches the lineage, that the matrix labels match the taxa records, that the matrix is symmetric, and that every stored distance agrees with the stored lineages under the stored metric. Using a bundle in memory (printing it or passing it to distance_matrix()) checks its structure only.

title: Bundle format
text:
Example
The example bundle was produced offline from three curated lineages:

res <- taxo_from_lineages(
  list(
    Tyrannosaurus = c("Biota", "Animalia", "Chordata", "Dinosauria", "Theropoda", "Tyrannosaurus"),
    Velociraptor  = c("Biota", "Animalia", "Chordata", "Dinosauria", "Theropoda", "Velociraptor"),
    Homo          = c("Biota", "Animalia", "Chordata", "Mammalia", "Primates", "Homo")
  ),
  ranks = list(
    Tyrannosaurus = c(NA, "Kingdom", "Phylum", NA, NA, "Genus"),
    Velociraptor  = c(NA, "Kingdom", "Phylum", NA, NA, "Genus"),
    Homo          = c(NA, "Kingdom", "Phylum", "Class", "Order", "Genus")
  )
)

bundle

#> • Resolved: 3

#> • Unresolved: 0

write_taxodist_bundle(bundle, file)
distance_matrix(read_taxodist_bundle(file))

Distance matrices
R stores only the lower triangle in a compact dist object. Convert it when a square matrix is required:
d <- distance_matrix(taxa)
m <- as.matrix(d)

Julia returns a square labeled matrix type directly:

title: Cross-language Compatibility
text:
Clustering and ordination
The analysis results are semantically aligned but use different numerical ecosystems.

Clustering
R delegates to stats::hclust(). Since version 1.1.0, Python and Julia use ports of the Fortran routines of stats::hclust(), so merges, heights, and leaf order equal R’s for every method, also when distances are tied. The results are still returned in each ecosystem’s structure: a SciPy linkage matrix in Python (alongside R’s merge, height, and order) and a Clustering.Hclust in Julia; plotting defaults differ.


Ordination
All three implementations perform classical multidimensional scaling and return:

points;
the underlying dist or distance DataFrame;
GOF goodness-of-fit values;
eig eigenvalues.

Coordinate signs may differ between numerical implementations because eigenvectors are defined only up to sign. A sign reversal of an axis does not change the represented geometry or pairwise distances.






NoteCompare geometry, not axis orientation



When validating ordinations across languages, compare eigenvalues and Euclidean distances among coordinates. Do not require every coordinate column to have the same sign.

title: Cross-language Compatibility

Plotting and console output
R uses S3 methods such as print(), plot(), and summary(). Python and Julia expose explicit helpers such as plot_taxodist_cluster(), plot_taxodist_ord(), and summary_taxodist_ord(). Plotting is optional in both: Python needs pip install "taxodist[plot]", and Julia loads its plotting code only after using Plots.
Typography, plotting backends, colors, dendrogram orientation, and console formatting are not part of the cross-language compatibility contract. Scientific values, labels, and structural fields are.

Cache compatibility
Cache contents have the same conceptual keys—resolved IDs and lineages—but the files are intentionally not interchangeable:

R uses saveRDS() and .rds files;
Python uses pickle and .pkl files;
Julia uses JSON and .json files.

Do not rename one format to imitate another. For a cross-language archival record, use the portable bundle format introduced in version 0.8.0.
In all three implementations, cleaned and uncleaned lineages are cached under separate keys (lin_<id> and rawlin_<id>), as are their ranks (ranks_<id> and rawranks_<id>), and save_cache() and load_cache() default to a persistent per-user location when no file is given. Cache files record the parser version (meta_parser_version); lineages from files written before version 1.0.0 are discarded on loading, and their taxon identifiers are kept.

Only load .pkl files from trusted sources. Python’s pickle format can execute code during deserialization.

title: taxodist
text:
Taxonomic hierarchy distances and lineage analysis in R, Python, and Julia
taxodist retrieves ordered taxonomic lineages and the ranks of their nodes from The Taxonomicon, the Open Tree Taxonomy, or the NCBI Taxonomy, documents name-resolution decisions, and computes distances from the depth of the most recent common ancestor in the continuous shared lineage prefix. Path-length, Wu–Palmer, and rank-based distances and the taxonomic distinctness indices of Clarke and Warwick are also available.
Introduction and usage · Methodology · Function reference · Web application

title: taxodist
text:
What does taxodist measure?
For two ordered lineages \(L_A\) and \(L_B\), taxodist finds their continuous common prefix. Its final node is their most recent common ancestor (MRCA):
\[
d(A,B)=
\begin{cases}
0, & L_A = L_B, \\
\dfrac{1}{\operatorname{depth}(\operatorname{MRCA})}, & L_A \neq L_B.
\end{cases}
\]
A deeper shared ancestor produces a smaller distance. Zero is reserved for identical hierarchy nodes; distinct ancestor–descendant nodes retain a positive distance. This reciprocal distance is the default; the metric argument selects the path length, the Wu–Palmer distance, or a rank-based distance instead.






ImportantClassification distance, not evolutionary distance



These values describe separation within a recorded classification. They are not evolutionary time, genetic distance, morphological divergence, phylogenetic branch length, or evidence that a particular phylogeny is correct.


Detailed definition and assumptions

title: taxodist
text:
Version 1.1.0
Version 1.1.0, for R, Python, and Julia, adds taxonomic sources and community analyses. The distance metrics and the bundle format are unchanged, and distances computed from The Taxonomicon are identical to version 1.0.0 (except for the rare pages without a structured hierarchy).

Three taxonomic sources. taxo_resolve() and taxo_bundle() gain a source argument: besides The Taxonomicon (default), lineages can come from the Open Tree of Life reference taxonomy ("ott") and the NCBI Taxonomy ("ncbi"). Identifiers carry a source prefix, and resolutions and bundles record the source and its version. taxo_sources() lists the sources with their citations. Taxonomic sources
How much does the classification matter? compare_sources() resolves the same taxa in several sources and reports the agreement between their distance matrices (Spearman correlation and Mantel test).
Community analyses. taxo_dissimilarity() computes the taxonomic dissimilarities Γ+ and Θ+ between samples (Clarke et al. 2006), and taxo_ses() the standardized effect sizes NRI and NTI (Webb et al. 2002). Community analyses
Homonyms. A nominotypical subgenus such as Mus (Mus) is no longer counted as a homonym of its genus, so names such as "Mus" resolve without ambiguity.
Faster matrices. Common-ancestor depths are computed from a sorted index of the lineages; results are identical and large matrices are several times faster.

title: taxodist
text:
Version 1.0.0
Version 1.0.0 is the first stable release, published simultaneously for R, Python, and Julia. The default distance, the alternative metrics, and the bundle format (schema 1.1) are now stable: later 1.x releases keep their definitions and continue to read bundles written by this version.

New lineage parser. Lineages are read from the structure of The Taxonomicon page rather than from its text, so author strings, rank labels, and markers can no longer leak into, or remove, lineage nodes. Distances can differ from earlier versions.
Ranks. The rank of every lineage node is retrieved and cached with the lineage. lineage_ranks() returns each node with its rank and depth, and resolutions store the ranks.
Distance metrics. A metric argument selects "reciprocal" (default, unchanged), "path", "wu_palmer", or "ranked" (Clarke and Warwick’s step weights).
Taxonomic distinctness. taxo_distinctness() computes Δ, Δ*, Δ+, and Λ+ (agreeing with vegan::taxondive()), and taxo_distinctness_test() compares a sample with random draws from a species pool.
Bundle schema 1.1. Bundles record the metric and the lineage ranks; schema 1.0 bundles are still read.
Gentler on the server. Consecutive requests are spaced by at least 0.25 s, and taxonomicon_available() checks quickly whether the server can be reached.

See the changelog for the complete list, including breaking changes.

title: Changelog
text:
taxodist 1.1.0 Latest
Lineages can now come from three classifications, the dependence of an analysis on the classification can be measured, and community analyses gain taxonomic dissimilarity between samples and standardized effect sizes. The distance metrics and the bundle format (schema 1.1) are unchanged: distances computed from The Taxonomicon are identical to version 1.0.0 (except for the rare pages without a structured hierarchy; see Corrections), and bundles written by either version are read by both.

Released — R: 2026-11-26 on CRAN · Python: 2026-11-25 on PyPI · Julia: registered in Julia General


New taxonomic sources

taxo_resolve() and taxo_bundle() gain a source argument. Besides The Taxonomicon ("taxonomicon", the default), lineages can be retrieved from the Open Tree of Life reference taxonomy ("ott") and the NCBI Taxonomy ("ncbi"), through their public APIs. The resulting resolutions work with every function that accepts one: distance_matrix(), cross_distances(), taxo_tree(), taxo_bundle(), and, through the matrix, taxo_distinctness(). Identifiers carry a source prefix ("ott:770309", "ncbi:9606"), ranks are recorded in the same form as for The Taxonomicon, and the resolution and its bundles record the source and, for the Open Tree Taxonomy, its version.
Requests to each source are spaced independently. NCBI requests are spaced by at least 0.4 s, below its limit of three per second (0.12 s with an API key, set in the NCBI_API_KEY environment variable, or options(taxodist.ncbi_api_key) in R, taxodist.sources.NCBI_API_KEY in Python, Taxodist.NCBI_API_KEY[] in Julia), and refused requests (HTTP 429) are retried after a pause.
taxo_sources() lists the supported sources with their licence and citation.
compare_sources() resolves the same taxa in several sources and reports the lineage depth of every taxon in each, and the agreement between their distance matrices (Spearman correlation and Mantel permutation test), i.e. how much an analysis depends on the classification it is based on.
See Taxonomic sources.



Community analyses

taxo_dissimilarity() computes the taxonomic dissimilarities Γ+ and Θ+ of Clarke, Somerfield and Chapman (2006) between samples, for ordination, clustering, or PERMANOVA. They credit closely related taxa as near matches, so samples without any taxon in common can still be compared; on a flat classification they reduce to the presence/absence Bray–Curtis (Sørensen) and Kulczynski dissimilarities, which the tests verify against vegan::vegdist().
taxo_ses() computes the standardized effect sizes of the mean pairwise distance (NRI) and the mean nearest-taxon distance (NTI) of Webb et al. (2002) on taxonomic distances, under a species-pool null model or the independent swap, optionally weighted by abundance as in the picante package.
See Community analyses.



Name resolution

A candidate nested in another candidate of the same name, such as the nominotypical subgenus Mus (Mus) inside the genus Mus, is no longer counted as a homonym, in taxo_resolve() and in name-based functions. Names such as "Mus", "Oncorhynchus", or "Leishmania" are therefore resolved instead of ambiguous, and no homonym warning is emitted for them. The lineage is unchanged, since it was already truncated at the queried name.



Performance

distance_matrix() and cross_distances(), and therefore taxo_cluster(), taxo_ordinate(), taxo_heatmap(), taxo_bundle(), and taxo_distinctness(), compute common-ancestor depths with a sorted index of the lineages: in lexicographic order, the common prefix of two lineages is the minimum of the common prefixes of the neighbouring lineages between them. The depths from one taxon to all others then take two cumulative minima instead of a node-by-node comparison of every pair. Results are identical. In R, a matrix of 2000 taxa is about 10 times faster (5000 taxa: 27 s to 2 s); in Python, a matrix of 5000 taxa is about 4 times faster (3.7 s to 0.9 s); in Julia, 5000 synthetic taxa take about 0.22–0.25 s instead of 0.41–0.65 s.



Corrections

The plain-text fallback parser, used for pages without the structured hierarchy block, kept the no-break spaces that indent The Taxonomicon tree, so rank labels were not removed and nodes such as "Clade" or "Domain" could enter the lineage (R and Julia). A shared fixture (expected_text_fallback.json) now checks the three implementations.
Taxon names are normalized with Unicode whitespace, such as the no-break space, as well as ASCII whitespace.
R: write_taxodist_bundle() writes distances with 17 significant digits, so they are read back exactly, as in the Python and Julia writers. Previously 15 digits were used.



Behavior changes

metric must be a single string. In R a vector of several metrics was silently reduced to its first element; it is now an error, as in Python and Julia, with the same message in the three implementations.
compare_bundles() reports the metric of each bundle (metric_old, metric_new) and whether it changed (metric_changed), and its printed form warns when the distances are not comparable.
The HTTP user agent follows a format shared by the three implementations: taxodist/<version> (<language>; +https://taxodist.github.io).



Python-specific changes

compare_sources() and taxo_ses() take seed= for reproducible random draws; print_taxodist_ses() prints an effect-size table with its settings. taxo_dissimilarity() returns a square pandas.DataFrame (attrs["method"], attrs["metric"]).
taxo_cluster() reproduces R’s stats::hclust() exactly (a port of R’s Fortran routines): merges, heights, and leaf order equal R’s for all eight methods, including tied distances, and "ward.D", "ward.D2", and "mcquitty" are accepted. "hclust" is still a SciPy linkage matrix; the result also contains R’s "merge", "height", and "order".
closest_relative() and focal_distances() keep the input order of tied distances.
taxo_bundle() labels a resolution without a source as coming from The Taxonomicon, as R does, instead of raising an error.
The package defines __all__, listing the public API.



Julia-specific changes

compare_sources() and taxo_ses() take rng (for example Random.Xoshiro(1)) for reproducible random draws. taxo_dissimilarity() returns a TaxonomicDistanceMatrix between samples whose new method field records the index; taxo_ses() returns a TaxodistSES; compare_sources() returns a TaxodistSourceComparison. NCBI’s XML is read by a small internal reader, so no dependency was added.
taxo_cluster() uses a port of R’s stats::hclust() instead of Clustering.jl’s hclust(), so merges, heights, and leaf order equal R’s for every method, also with tied distances. "mcquitty", "median", and "centroid" are now available, and "ward.D" and "ward.D2" are accepted. The result still holds a Clustering.Hclust.
focal_distances() gives a missing mrca_depth for a community taxon that cannot be found, instead of 0.
ambiguity must be exactly "warn", "first", or "error", as in Python.
taxo_distinctness() returns a TaxodistDistinctness, displayed like R’s printed result; its metric and data fields, indexing by name, and destructuring work as before.

title: Changelog
text:
taxodist 1.0.0
First stable release, published simultaneously for R, Python, and Julia. The default distance metric, the other metrics, and the bundle format (schema 1.1) are now stable: later 1.x releases will keep their definitions and continue to read bundles written by this version.

Released — R: 2026-11-06 on CRAN · Python: 2026-11-05 on PyPI · Julia: registered in Julia General


New features

Ranks. The rank of every lineage node (for example "Kingdom", "Clade", "Superfamily", or "Genus") is read from The Taxonomicon and cached with the lineage. The new lineage_ranks() returns each node with its rank and depth. taxo_resolve() results gain a ranks column, and taxo_from_lineages() accepts user-supplied ranks through a new ranks argument.
Distance metrics. taxo_distance(), distance_matrix(), cross_distances(), closest_relative(), focal_distances(), taxo_heatmap(), and taxo_bundle() gain a metric argument, which taxo_cluster() and taxo_ordinate() pass on to distance_matrix():

"reciprocal" (default): \(1/\operatorname{depth}(\operatorname{MRCA})\), unchanged;
"path": the number of edges between the two nodes in the classification tree;
"wu_palmer": \(1 - 2\operatorname{depth}(\operatorname{MRCA}) / (\operatorname{depth}(A) + \operatorname{depth}(B))\), which normalizes for the uneven resolution of different parts of the classification;
"ranked": half the path length through the standard Linnaean ranks only (kingdom to species, configurable), i.e. the step weights of Clarke and Warwick.

Distance matrices record the metric used (the "method" attribute of the R dist, attrs["metric"] in Python, and the metric field in Julia), and taxo_distance() results gain a metric element.
Taxonomic distinctness. taxo_distinctness() computes Warwick and Clarke’s taxonomic diversity (Δ), distinctness (Δ*), average taxonomic distinctness (Δ+), and its variation (Λ+) for one or more samples, from presence or abundance data. Results agree with vegan::taxondive(). taxo_distinctness_test() compares Δ+ and Λ+ of a sample with random samples of the same size from a master list.
taxonomicon_available() reports whether The Taxonomicon can be reached, with a short timeout. R examples that need the server now run only when it answers, so checking the package no longer waits on network timeouts.
Bundle schema 1.1. Bundles record the metric used (and, for "ranked", its rank levels) and the lineage ranks. Distances are verified with the stored metric. Schema 1.0 bundles are still read and must use the reciprocal metric.



Breaking changes: lineage parsing






ImportantDistances can differ from earlier versions



Lineages are now read from the structure of The Taxonomicon page instead of its text. Each node’s name is taken from the page’s own markup for the scientific name, so author strings, rank labels, extinction and type markers, and vernacular names can no longer leak into, or remove, nodes. Previously about 16% of lineages contained malformed nodes such as "Passeres (C.", "Delphinida de", or "Alismatales R.Br. ex"; because these contained spaces, name-based queries silently dropped them, so lineage depths, and therefore distances, differed from the classification and from ID-based queries. Some clades were also lost entirely (for example Terrestrornithes, Dendrornithes, and Anomalogonates in passerine birds), taxa whose page row is labelled [plesion] or Anamorph genus were recorded under that label, and the ‡ marker was not removed. Analyses computed with earlier versions should be recomputed.



Species are now recorded as nodes of their subspecies, and subgenera as nodes of their species, when they appear in the lineage. Previously "Subspecies Homo sapiens sapiens" was parsed as "Subspecies" and the species node was dropped.
Pages without the structured hierarchy block are still parsed from text, now by extracting the scientific name at the start of each line rather than by deleting author strings. This handles lower-case particles (de, van der, d'), non-ASCII initials (Özdikmen), and abbreviations (R.Br. ex).
The parser is identical in the three implementations and is checked against the same trimmed copies of real Taxonomicon pages and their expected lineages.
The taxobase reference dataset was rebuilt with the new parser.



Corrections

Taxon names containing regular-expression metacharacters, notably parentheses in subgenus names such as "Microtus (Agricola)", are matched literally. Whole-word matching no longer fails next to punctuation and recognizes non-ASCII letters.
taxo_resolve() reports a name whose candidates were all retrieved but are not biological (for example astronomical objects) as "unresolved" instead of "retrieval_error".
When a name has several biological entries, entries marked as invalid, rejected, nude, or illegitimate names (nom. inval., nom. rej., nom. nud., nom. illeg.) are considered only after the others. Previously "Amanita" resolved to an invalid name instead of the conserved genus.
load_cache() discards lineages from cache files written by earlier versions, whose parser could produce malformed nodes, and keeps their taxon IDs. save_cache() records the parser version in the file.
Python: resolutions are no longer mistaken for distance matrices by taxo_cluster() and taxo_ordinate(); returned lineages are copies, so modifying them no longer corrupts the cache; a single string passed where several taxa are expected is treated as one taxon; integral numbers are treated as Taxonomicon IDs.
Julia: the 30-second HTTP timeout is applied again; numeric taxa no longer cause errors in the pairwise and focal functions; taxo_from_lineages() keeps the order of a vector of label => lineage pairs (a plain Dict is sorted by label); the session cache is safe to use from several tasks or threads.



Network

Consecutive requests to The Taxonomicon are spaced by at least 0.25 seconds, so large batches do not overload the server. The interval is set with options(taxodist.min_interval = ...) in R, taxodist.fetch.MIN_INTERVAL in Python, and Taxodist.MIN_INTERVAL[] in Julia; 0 disables it.



Packaging

R: xml2 moved from Suggests to Imports.
Python: matplotlib and seaborn are now optional and installed with pip install "taxodist[plot]"; Python 3.8 is no longer supported. The bundle JSON schema is included in the package.
Julia: Plots.jl is now a weak dependency loaded through a package extension, so using Taxodist no longer loads Plots; run using Plots to enable plotting.

title: Changelog
text:
taxodist 0.9.0
Version 0.9.0 was released simultaneously for R, Python, and Julia. The distance definition and the bundle schema (version 1.0) are unchanged; bundles written by any of the three implementations are read by the other two without differences.

Released — R: 2026-10-12 (CRAN archive) · Python: 2026-10-12 on PyPI · Julia: registered in Julia General


Corrections

taxo_resolve() now truncates each selected lineage at the queried taxon exactly as get_lineage() does. Previously it stored the lineage of the retrieved page unchanged; for genera whose page does not list the genus itself (for example Periplaneta), the lineage ended at the family, resolved_name reported the family, and distance_matrix(taxo_resolve(x)) could differ from distance_matrix(x). Bundles built from such resolutions inherited the difference.
Cleaned and uncleaned lineages are cached separately. A call with clean = FALSE previously replaced the cleaned entry, so later calls returned nodes above Biota for the rest of the session.
Queried names are normalized (surrounding and repeated whitespace) and located in the lineage without regard to letter case. Previously "tyrannosaurus" or "Tyrannosaurus " added a spurious terminal node, increasing lineage depth.
taxo_heatmap() passes plotting arguments only to the plotting function (R and Julia previously forwarded them to distance_matrix(); Python rejected cmap and annot). verbose and progress are explicit arguments.
cache_info() reports the names of cached taxa together with their identifiers (ids); it previously listed identifiers only.
get_lineage_by_id() accepts numeric identifiers and reports an informative error for several identifiers.
Python: the User-Agent header and bundle metadata report the installed version, distance_matrix() rejects a single string, and each candidate lineage is retrieved once during disambiguation.



Behavior changes






ImportantChanged return values




check_coverage() reports an unknown result (NA in R, pd.NA in Python, missing in Julia) when The Taxonomicon could not be reached. Such names were previously reported as absent.
save_cache() returns the path of the written file.
Using a bundle in distance_matrix() or printing it validates its structure only. The complete recomputation of every stored distance is performed when a bundle is written or read.





New functions and arguments

taxo_tree() builds a tree directly from lineages. Internal nodes are the named clades at which the supplied taxa diverge; clades with a single descendant are collapsed. Branch lengths place a clade at depth \(h\) at height \(1/(2h)\), so the tree is ultrametric and its patristic distances equal distance_matrix(). R returns an ape-compatible phylo object; Python and Julia return a TaxodistTree with Newick export.
cross_distances(x, y) computes the rectangular matrix between two sets of taxa.
compare_bundles(old, new) classifies every input as unchanged, added, removed, or changed in status, identifier, or lineage, and lists the pairwise distances that changed. Bundle files can be passed by path.
taxo_resolve() and taxo_bundle() gain within, which restricts candidates to those whose lineage contains a given clade.
save_cache() and load_cache() default to a persistent per-user cache file.



Performance and network handling

Distance matrices are computed from integer prefix identifiers: each node is mapped to an integer identifying its complete path from the root, so the MRCA depth of two taxa is the number of depths at which the identifiers agree.
Requests are retried with exponential backoff after network errors and server errors (5xx); the number of attempts is configurable.



Web application

The application uses the 0.9.0 packages, adds a between-groups tab and classification trees, reports names that were not found and the entry chosen for ambiguous names, offers CSV, PNG, Newick, and bundle downloads, and supports links that reopen a query.
Its bundled lineage cache was rebuilt; a cache produced by an earlier parser is no longer loaded.

Version 0.9.0 validation and performance

Bundle interoperability
Release 0.9.0 was checked with a common set of user-supplied lineages that included an ancestor–descendant pair, two inputs with identical lineages, and a lineage with a different root (infinite distances). title: Taxonomic Sources
text: A taxonomic distance is a property of the classification it is computed from. Since version 1.1.0, taxodist can retrieve lineages from three classifications, and compare_sources() measures how much the distances among a set of taxa change from one classification to another.

title: Taxonomic Sources
text:
The three sources

library(taxodist)

taxo_sources()[, c("id", "name", "id_prefix")]
#>            id               name id_prefix
#> 1 taxonomicon    The Taxonomicon          
#> 2         ott Open Tree Taxonomy      ott:
#> 3        ncbi      NCBI Taxonomy     ncbi:

The Taxonomicon is a single curated classification with very deep lineages, many unranked clades, and extensive fossil coverage. It remains the default, and every name-based function (get_lineage(), taxo_distance(), distance_matrix() on names, and so on) looks names up there.
The Open Tree Taxonomy synthesizes NCBI, GBIF, WoRMS, IRMNG, and other taxonomies.
The NCBI Taxonomy covers organisms with sequence data.

taxo_sources() also returns the URL, licence, and preferred citation of every source. Cite the source your lineages come from (see About).

title: Taxonomic Sources
text:
Choosing a source
The other sources are selected with the source argument of taxo_resolve() and taxo_bundle():

RPythonJulia


library(taxodist)

apes <- c("Homo", "Pan", "Gorilla", "Pongo", "Hylobates")
ott  <- taxo_resolve(apes, source = "ott")
ncbi <- taxo_resolve(apes, source = "ncbi")

ott$id                       # prefixed identifiers, e.g. "ott:770309" for Homo
attr(ott, "source")          # the source, with the Open Tree Taxonomy version

distance_matrix(ott)
taxo_tree(ncbi)
bundle <- taxo_bundle(ott)   # the bundle records the source and its version


import taxodist as td

apes = ["Homo", "Pan", "Gorilla", "Pongo", "Hylobates"]
ott = td.taxo_resolve(apes, source="ott")
ncbi = td.taxo_resolve(apes, source="ncbi")

ott["id"]                    # prefixed identifiers, e.g. "ott:770309" for Homo
ott.source, ott.source_url   # the source, with the Open Tree Taxonomy version

td.distance_matrix(ott)
td.taxo_tree(ncbi)
bundle = td.taxo_bundle(ott)  # the bundle records the source and its version


using Taxodist

apes = ["Homo", "Pan", "Gorilla", "Pongo", "Hylobates"]
ott = taxo_resolve(apes; source="ott")
ncbi = taxo_resolve(apes; source="ncbi")

ott.source, ott.source_url   # the source, with the Open Tree Taxonomy version

distance_matrix(ott)
taxo_tree(ncbi)
bundle = taxo_bundle(ott)    # the bundle records the source and its version



A resolution from any source works with every function that accepts a resolution: distance_matrix(), cross_distances(), taxo_tree(), taxo_bundle(), and, through the matrix, taxo_distinctness(), taxo_dissimilarity(), and taxo_ses(). taxo_bundle() with source resolves the names and builds the bundle in one step.

Identifiers
Identifiers stored in resolutions and bundles carry a source prefix: "ott:770309" for an Open Tree Taxonomy identifier and "ncbi:9606" for an NCBI identifier. Taxonomicon identifiers have no prefix. When source is set, an identifier can be passed with or without its prefix (taxo_resolve("9606", source = "ncbi") and taxo_resolve("ncbi:9606", source = "ncbi") are equivalent). Identifiers are specific to one source.


Ranks and provenance
Ranks are recorded in the same form as for The Taxonomicon (the ranks column of the resolution). The resolution records the name and URL of its source; for the Open Tree Taxonomy, the name includes the version of the taxonomy served by the API at the time of retrieval. Bundles copy this into their source field, so a bundle documents which classification, and which version of it, its distances were computed from. See Bundle Format.


Clade names and within
Clade names differ between classifications, which matters for the within argument: animals are "Animalia" in The Taxonomicon but "Metazoa" in the Open Tree and NCBI taxonomies.

RPythonJulia


taxo_resolve("Nereis", within = "Animalia")                  # The Taxonomicon
taxo_resolve("Nereis", within = "Metazoa", source = "ncbi")  # NCBI Taxonomy


td.taxo_resolve(["Nereis"], within="Animalia")                 # The Taxonomicon
td.taxo_resolve(["Nereis"], within="Metazoa", source="ncbi")   # NCBI Taxonomy


taxo_resolve(["Nereis"]; within="Animalia")                  # The Taxonomicon
taxo_resolve(["Nereis"]; within="Metazoa", source="ncbi")    # NCBI Taxonomy



compare_sources() accepts one within clade per source for this reason (see below).

title: Taxonomic Sources
section: Request limits and the NCBI API key
text:
Request limits and the NCBI API key
Requests to each source are spaced independently, by at least the minimum interval (0.25 s by default; see Settings). The NCBI E-utilities allow three requests per second without an API key and ten with one, so NCBI requests are spaced by at least 0.4 s, or 0.12 s with a key. Refused requests (HTTP 429) are retried after a pause.
An NCBI API key is free with an NCBI account. Set it in the NCBI_API_KEY environment variable, which the three implementations read, or in the session:

RPythonJulia


Sys.setenv(NCBI_API_KEY = "your-key")
# or
options(taxodist.ncbi_api_key = "your-key")


import taxodist.sources
taxodist.sources.NCBI_API_KEY = "your-key"


Taxodist.NCBI_API_KEY[] = "your-key"



Keep the key out of scripts that you share; setting it in the environment avoids writing it in code.

title: Taxonomic Sources
section: How much does the classification matter?
text:
How much does the classification matter?
compare_sources() resolves the same names in several sources and reports how deep each lineage is in each one, and how well their distance matrices agree:

RPythonJulia


cmp <- compare_sources(
  c("Homo", "Pan", "Mus", "Gallus", "Danio", "Drosophila", "Quercus"),
  sources = c("taxonomicon", "ott", "ncbi")
)
cmp            # summary
cmp$taxa       # status, identifier, and lineage depth in each source
cmp$agreement  # one row per pair of sources


cmp = td.compare_sources(
    ["Homo", "Pan", "Mus", "Gallus", "Danio", "Drosophila", "Quercus"],
    sources=["taxonomicon", "ott", "ncbi"],
    seed=1,
)
print(cmp)     # summary
cmp.taxa       # status, identifier, and lineage depth in each source
cmp.agreement  # one row per pair of sources


using Random

cmp = compare_sources(
    ["Homo", "Pan", "Mus", "Gallus", "Danio", "Drosophila", "Quercus"];
    sources=["taxonomicon", "ott", "ncbi"],
    rng=Xoshiro(1),
)
cmp            # summary (REPL display)
cmp.taxa       # status, identifier, and lineage depth in each source
cmp.agreement  # one row per pair of sources



The input must contain at least three names (identifiers are specific to one source and are not accepted), and sources at least two sources. Names are resolved with ambiguity = "first" by default, so ambiguity is reported in the status columns rather than as warnings. within is one clade name for every source or one per source, for example c(taxonomicon = "Animalia", ott = "Metazoa", ncbi = "Metazoa") in R.

Interpreting the result

taxa has one row per input and, for every source, its status (status_<source>), selected identifier (id_<source>), and lineage depth (depth_<source>). Check the statuses first: a name that is "unresolved" or "ambiguous" in one source may refer to a different organism, or to none, there.
agreement has one row per pair of sources: the number of taxa compared (n_taxa, the taxa resolved in every source, listed in shared), the Spearman correlation between the two sets of pairwise distances (spearman), and the p-value of a Mantel permutation test (p_value). The test permutes the taxa of one matrix and reports the proportion of permutations whose correlation is at least the observed one, counting the observed arrangement: \((1 + \text{count}) / (1 + \text{permutations})\). Set permutations = 0 to skip it.
matrices holds the distance matrices of every source restricted to the shared taxa, and resolutions the full resolutions.

A correlation close to 1 means that the classifications rank the pairs of taxa in nearly the same order, so conclusions based on relative distances are robust to the choice of source. A low correlation points to parts of the tree of life that the classifications resolve differently, and the depth columns show where. Lineage depths, and therefore absolute distances, are not comparable across sources, because each classification resolves different groups to different degrees (The Taxonomicon is usually much deeper); compare correlations, not raw values. With few taxa the Mantel test has little power, and its p-value is limited by the number of distinct permutations.
The p-values come from random permutations: use set.seed() in R, seed in Python, and rng in Julia for reproducible values. The permutations differ between languages, so p-values can differ slightly; the correlations, depths, and matrices are identical.

title: Taxonomic Sources
text:
Homonyms and nominotypical subgenera
A name can match several taxa. Since version 1.1.0, a candidate nested in another candidate of the same name is not counted as a homonym: the nominotypical subgenus Mus (Mus) lies inside the genus Mus, so "Mus" resolves to the genus with status = "resolved" instead of "ambiguous", and no homonym warning is emitted. The same applies to names such as "Oncorhynchus" or "Leishmania", and to subspecies with the same name as their species. The lineage is unchanged, since it was already truncated at the queried name. The rule applies in every source, in taxo_resolve(), and in the name-based functions.
True homonyms, such as Drosophila (a fly and a fungus in the NCBI Taxonomy) or Nereis (a polychaete and a butterfly in The Taxonomicon), remain "ambiguous". Restrict them with within or pass an identifier.
